lead: This unit is about the instruments that look inside the body to diagnose, and about the electrical rules that keep the patient alive while they work. After it you can read a pure-tone audiogram, follow light and image through an endoscope, use the Imbert-Fick idea to check a tonometer reading, and decide from current, path and duration whether a shock is macro or micro. You can also list the safety tests a biomedical technician runs on a machine and say which risk class the device falls into.
about: This unit covers the instruments that look at the body rather than treat it, and the safety rules around every machine in a hospital. 6.1 starts with pure-tone audiometry, 6.2 shows how an endoscope carries light in and an image out, and 6.3 covers the dental X-ray tube. The unit then turns to danger: 6.4 explains how current harms the body at macro- and micro-shock levels, and 6.5 turns those thresholds into grounding, isolation and leakage tests. 6.6 shows where the electrical safety standard sits inside medical device regulation. The last two chapters return to measurement: 6.7 records skin resistance and other autonomic signals in a polygraph, and 6.8 covers tonometers, slit lamps and auto refractometers in the eye clinic.

chapters.idea: An audiometer is a calibrated tone generator plus headphones: it finds the softest level a person hears at each frequency and plots it as a hearing level in dB HL.
chapters.depth: Air conduction through headphones and bone conduction through a vibrator on the mastoid; the audiogram from 125 Hz to 8 kHz with hearing level on the vertical axis; the Hughson-Westlake staircase (drop 10 dB after a heard tone, raise 5 dB after a miss) to find threshold; masking of the non-test ear with narrow-band noise; calibration, with 0 dB HL fixed at a reference pressure (20 µPa at 1 kHz) that differs at every frequency; a short look at speech audiometry (some syllabi call it speech reception threshold testing). Keep circuit detail light.

figure.aria: Hearing level against frequency: a flat line at 0 dB HL for normal ears and a patient curve rising from 20 dB at 250 Hz to 60 dB at 4000 Hz.

chapters.example: A pure-tone audiometer is calibrated so that 0 dB HL at 1 kHz equals a sound pressure of 20 µPa. A patient hears the 1 kHz tone only when the dial is at 60 dB HL. What pressure reached the ear? Answer: level in dB = 20 log₁₀(p/p₀), so p = p₀ × 10^(60/20) = 20 µPa × 1000 = 20,000 µPa = 20 mPa, a thousand times the reference pressure.
chapters.trap: dB HL is not dB SPL. A reading of 40 dB HL means 40 dB above the normal threshold at that frequency, not a fixed pressure, because the reference pressure changes with frequency.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: bio-amplifiers, filters and recorders (the tone generator, attenuator and output stage reuse those ideas)
chapters.leave: Impedance audiometry and otoacoustic emissions to an audiology paper; evoked-potential audiometry belongs with evoked potentials in Unit 1

chapters.idea: An endoscope pipes light into a cavity along one bundle of fibres and brings the image back along a second, coherent bundle or a tiny camera at the tip.
chapters.depth: Rigid endoscope with a rod-lens train, flexible fibre-optic endoscope, and video endoscope with a CCD or CMOS sensor at the tip; illumination by a xenon or LED lamp through a non-coherent fibre bundle; image through a coherent bundle that keeps fibre positions the same at both ends; working channels for biopsy forceps, suction and water; tip angulation by cables; why each type gets a different sterilisation method; the main uses (gastroscopy, colonoscopy, bronchoscopy, laparoscopy, cystoscopy, arthroscopy) and one line on capsule endoscopy.

figure.title: Light path in a flexible endoscope
figure.aria: Block diagram of a flexible endoscope: lamp to light bundle to tissue to objective lens to image bundle to processor to monitor.

chapters.example: A flexible endoscope has 10,000 image fibres, each with core diameter 30 µm. Find the total light-carrying area. Core radius = 15 µm, area per fibre = π × 15² ≈ 707 µm². Total = 10,000 × 707 = 7.07 × 10⁶ µm² = 7.07 mm². A larger core carries more light but gives a coarser picture, because two points closer than one fibre width cannot be told apart.
chapters.trap: Swapping the two bundles. The incoherent bundle only carries light; the coherent bundle carries the image because its fibres keep the same order at both ends.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: physiological transducers (a CCD at the tip is an image sensor of that family)
chapters.leave: Optical design of rod lenses, image processing and capsule-endoscope electronics to other courses

chapters.idea: A dental X-ray machine is a small, heavily shielded X-ray tube with a pointed cone that takes one short exposure of a tooth onto film or a digital sensor.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this, so keep it short. Stationary-anode tube with a tungsten target in oil, step-up transformer and timer; typical settings 60 to 70 kVp and 7 to 10 mA for 0.1 to 1 s, giving a few mAs; inherent and added filtration (about 2.5 mm aluminium), collimation to the cone, focal-spot size under 1 mm; film speed or digital sensor; the inverse-square law with cone length; lead apron and position-distance shielding for the operator; one line each on the intra-oral periapical and bitewing views, and on the panoramic (OPG) unit.

figure.title: Dental X-ray chain
figure.aria: Block diagram of a dental X-ray unit: timer and control, step-up transformer, tube, cone and filter, then the tooth and sensor.

chapters.example: A dental unit is set to 70 kVp, 7 mA and 0.6 s. (a) Find the exposure in mAs. (b) The cone is changed from 20 cm to 40 cm target-to-skin distance. By what factor does the skin dose change? (a) mAs = mA × s = 7 × 0.6 = 4.2 mAs. (b) Intensity follows 1/d², so dose falls by (40/20)² = 4; the new skin dose is one quarter of the old one.
chapters.trap: Mixing the two controls. kVp sets how penetrating the beam is and so the contrast, while mA sets how many X-rays are made; the timer and mA together give mAs.
chapters.prereq: Basic X-ray production and the inverse-square law from a first-year physics course
chapters.leave: Panoramic and cone-beam CT reconstruction to radiology courses; radiation dose limits to the radiation safety chapter in Unit 3

chapters.idea: The body is damaged by current, not by voltage, and the same current that only tingles through dry skin can fibrillate the heart when it reaches it through a catheter.
chapters.depth: Current paths through the body and the body model as resistance (about 1 to 10 kΩ hand-to-hand depending on skin wetness, a few hundred ohms internally); why 50/60 Hz is the most dangerous frequency; effects ladder: about 1 mA perception, 10 to 15 mA let-go, 20 to 30 mA respiratory tetanus, about 100 mA ventricular fibrillation for a shock of about a second; burns at the contact points; macro-shock (current through the intact skin) against micro-shock (10 to 100 µA straight into the heart through a catheter or an intracardiac electrode); duration and the vulnerable T-wave period; the 10 µA patient-leakage figure that safety design aims at.

figure.aria: Body current against touch voltage for dry and wet skin, with a flat line at the 100 mA fibrillation level that only the wet-skin line crosses.

chapters.example: A patient in a Chennai ICU touches a faulty 230 V casing. (a) Dry skin, 10 kΩ hand-to-hand: I = 230 / 10,000 = 23 mA, a painful but usually survivable shock. (b) Wet skin, 1 kΩ: I = 230 / 1000 = 230 mA, well above the 100 mA fibrillation level. (c) A catheter gives a 1 kΩ path to the heart and a 0.1 V offset appears across it: I = 0.1 / 1000 = 100 µA, above the micro-shock limit even though the voltage looks tiny.
chapters.trap: Quoting micro-shock limits in milliamps. The dangerous level for an intracardiac path is tens of microamps, about a thousand times smaller than the macro-shock fibrillation level.
chapters.prereq: First-year circuit ideas: V = I R, series and parallel paths
chapters.leave: Defibrillator protection circuits and pacemaker design to Unit 5; detailed standards values to chapter 6.5

chapters.idea: Electrical safety is proved by three defences (earthing, isolation and double insulation) and measured by four tests (inspection, earth continuity, insulation resistance and leakage current).
chapters.depth: Equipment classes I (protective earth), II (double insulation) and III (safety extra-low voltage); applied-part types B, BF and CF and what the F means (floating, isolated); protective earth wire and equipotential bonding; isolation transformer and the ELCB or GFCI; the difference between enclosure leakage current and patient leakage current; typical teaching limits: earth wire resistance ≤ 0.1 Ω, insulation resistance ≥ 1 MΩ at 500 V, earth leakage ≤ 5 mA, patient leakage ≤ 100 µA for type B or BF and ≤ 10 µA for type CF in normal condition, with higher single-fault figures; the test procedure with a safety analyser, including the single-fault test (earth open, neutral open); extra micro-shock precautions such as isolated patient inputs and one hand in the pocket.

figure.title: Order of safety tests
figure.aria: Flowchart of the safety check: visual inspection, earth continuity, insulation resistance, leakage current, functional test.

chapters.example: A technician tests a class I ventilator. Earth wire resistance reads 0.35 Ω, insulation resistance 50 MΩ, and earth leakage current 0.9 mA with the machine running. The limits are 0.1 Ω, 1 MΩ and 5 mA. Which test fails? Only the earth continuity, 0.35 Ω against 0.1 Ω, so the machine is taken out of service and the power cord earth pin is checked and repaired before the leakage test is trusted.
chapters.trap: Testing only in normal condition. Most dangerous faults are single faults (broken earth wire, broken neutral), and the single-fault leakage limit is the one the standard is really protecting the patient against.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.4: shock thresholds and the macro/micro-shock split
chapters.leave: Detailed clause-by-clause reading of the safety standard to a standards course; the regulatory paperwork to chapter 6.6

chapters.idea: A medical device may be sold only after its risk class decides how much evidence and which licence it needs.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this, so keep it short and rule-based. Risk classification by invasiveness, duration of contact and energy delivered; the Indian four-class scheme A to D under the Medical Devices Rules, 2017, administered by CDSCO, with licensing and quality management system requirements rising with the class; the US three-class scheme with 510(k) premarket notification and premarket approval; the CE mark route in Europe; the supporting standards, ISO 13485 for quality systems, ISO 14971 for risk management, IEC 60601-1 for electrical safety; clinical evaluation, labelling and instructions for use; post-market surveillance and adverse-event reporting. Do not quote form numbers or fees.

figure.aria: Decision tree that sends a non-invasive device to class A or B and an invasive or implanted device to class C or D.

chapters.example: Assign an Indian risk class and say which needs the most evidence: (i) a reusable stainless-steel tongue depressor, (ii) a sterile single-use hypodermic syringe, (iii) an implantable cardiac pacemaker. (i) Non-invasive, no energy: class A. (ii) Invasive, transient use: class B. (iii) Implanted, long contact: class D. The pacemaker carries the heaviest evidence load, including clinical investigation data and long-term post-market follow-up.
chapters.trap: Thinking price or brand sets the class. Class follows the rule chain: does it enter the body, how long does it stay, and how much energy does it deliver. A CE mark also does not replace an Indian licence.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.5: the electrical safety standard that appears in the regulatory file
chapters.leave: Drug regulation, clinical trial ethics and hospital purchase procedures to other papers

chapters.idea: Emotional arousal lowers skin resistance and changes breathing and pulse, so a polygraph records several such channels together and marks the moment each question was asked.
chapters.depth: Electrodermal activity, also called galvanic skin response (GSR) or the older psychogalvanic reflex; basal skin resistance (BSR) as the resting level, typically tens of kilo-ohms to about a megaohm across palm or finger electrodes; the GSR response as the fall in resistance after a stimulus, with a latency of about 1 to 3 s and a slow recovery; endosomatic and exosomatic measurement, the constant-current bridge method and electrode placement; the other polygraph channels: pneumograph chest and abdomen belts for respiration, a cuff or photoplethysmograph for cardiovascular change, sometimes an EMG channel; chart speed and artefacts from movement and sweat; one line that a polygraph measures arousal, not lying, and that courts in India treat the result as corroborative only.

figure.title: Polygraph channels
figure.aria: Block diagram of polygraph channels: breathing belts, palm electrodes and a cuff feed signal conditioners, and a question marker writes onto the same recorder.

chapters.example: A constant-current GSR meter passes 10 µA through palm electrodes. Across them the voltage is 1.5 V while the subject rests, and falls to 1.2 V just after a question. Find the basal skin resistance and the response. R = V/I, so basal = 1.5 / (10 × 10⁻⁶) = 150 kΩ, and after the question = 1.2 / (10 × 10⁻⁶) = 120 kΩ. The response is a fall of 30 kΩ, that is 20 per cent, and the meter reading must be inverted to plot resistance or the trace will look upside down.
chapters.trap: Writing that skin resistance rises with arousal. Sweat glands fill and conductance rises, so resistance falls; BSR is the resting level and the response is the change from it.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: surface electrodes and bio-amplifiers; chapter 6.4 for why a current through skin electrodes must stay small
chapters.leave: Lie-detection procedure and legal rules to a forensic paper; heart-rate and respiration measurement detail to Unit 2

chapters.idea: Each eye instrument measures one number: a tonometer measures pressure from force over a flattened area, the slit lamp gives an optical section of the eye, and the auto refractometer measures the lens power needed to focus the eye.
chapters.depth: Tonometry: indentation with a Schiotz tonometer and its conversion table, applanation with the Goldmann tonometer using the Imbert-Fick rule P = F/A, the fixed 3.06 mm applanation diameter, fluorescein and local anaesthetic, calibration checks, non-contact air-puff tonometry, and the normal intra-ocular pressure range of about 10 to 21 mmHg. Slit lamp: lamp arm, slit aperture, biomicroscope and joystick, bright and diffuse illumination, the optic section through cornea and lens, uses with a gonioscopy or fundus lens. Auto refractometer: infra-red target, Shack-Hartmann lenslet array or knife-edge detection, output of sphere, cylinder and axis, and the difference between refraction and visual acuity.

figure.title: Applanation tonometry
figure.aria: Four-step chain of applanation tonometry: tear film, prism flattening a 3.06 mm circle, force knob, then pressure by P = F/A.

chapters.example: A Goldmann prism flattens a circle of diameter 3.06 mm when the force knob is set to 20 mN. Find the intra-ocular pressure. Area = π r² = π × (1.53 mm)² = 7.35 mm² = 7.35 × 10⁻⁶ m². P = F/A = 20 × 10⁻³ / 7.35 × 10⁻⁶ = 2721 Pa. Since 1 mmHg = 133.3 Pa, P = 2721 / 133.3 = 20.4 mmHg, inside the normal range.
chapters.trap: Unit slips between mmHg and kPa, and millinewtons with newtons. Also, Imbert-Fick assumes a thin, dry, flexible cornea; the tear film pulls the prism in, which is why the area is fixed and the prism is calibrated.
chapters.prereq: Chapter 6.4 for patient-safe low-current design; basic lens optics (focal length, dioptre) from first-year physics
chapters.leave: Fundus cameras, perimetry and OCT to ophthalmology courses; the photoplethysmograph to Unit 2
